text:
Nearly 30 years after a violent clash between Native Americans and police, the Massachusetts town of Plymouth is in court accused of “silencing” their National Day of Mourning – again.
A Native American group won a “mixed” victory over the historic Massachusetts town of Plymouth after they sued them for breaking a 30-year-old ‘treaty’ involving their National Day of Mourning.
On Monday, the United American Indians of New England (UAINE) attended Plymouth superior court in the latest stage of a year-long dispute over who would fund the annual memorial, and whether Native Americans must “ask permission to protest on stolen land”.
While the judge ruled partially in their favour on Tuesday, Mahtowin Munro, an Oglala Lakota and co-leader of UAINE, warned that the fight was settler colonialism hiding behind “red tape” and that they did not expect justice from “the courts of colonizers”.
Jean-Luc Pierite, president of the North American Indian Centre of Boston (Naicob), told the Guardian: “This is political oppression. This is about holding government agencies to account for breach of contract, for breaking treaties.”
The National Day of Mourning (NDOM) was founded in 1970 by Wamsutta Frank James, a member of the federally recognised Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah) on Martha’s Vineyard, after he was uninvited from speaking at the state’s 350th anniversary of the Mayflower landing over his critical views.
For 50 years, as millions of Americans sit down to a turkey dinner, hundreds of Indigenous people and allies have gathered peacefully at noon on Cole’s Hill above Plymouth Rock in what is known as “America’s Hometown”, founded by the Pilgrims in 1620 on the ancestral Wampanoag homeland of Patuxet.
At the NDOM, food is shared, stories are told, and banners are paraded through the streets commemorating millions of Native Americans killed by European settlers, the theft of land, and the erasure of culture, as well as challenging Thanksgiving “myths”. UAINE call it a “solemn, spiritual and highly political day”.
In 1997, violence broke out. Town and state police were accused of pepper-spraying marchers, injuring elders, and arresting 25 people. Video footage from that day shows police hand-cuffing and dragging people.
A civil lawsuit ended in a 1998 out-of-court settlement allegedly amounting to $135,000 in which Plymouth agreed not to impede future NDOM protests, to provide a mobile stage, and to not require the organisation to ask for “permission to protest on stolen land”, including permits and prior notice.
In a statement at the time, UAINE said: “Plymouth has acknowledged our right to walk on our own land without a permit on National Day of Mourning. Plymouth has agreed to make the truth part of its celebration of the pilgrim myth of Thanksgiving … We are confident that this agreement represents a tremendous victory for the struggle of Native people to have our voices heard and respected.”
That all changed in 2025, when the town’s select board voted to renege on the agreement, and was overruled in court.
Munro said they suspected the town were “throwing up roadblocks because they don’t want the tourists to see or hear Native Americans who are speaking about the true history of the Pilgrim invasion and resulting land theft and genocide of Wampanoag and other Native peoples”.
On 10 November, 16 days before Thanksgiving, the board voted unanimously in a private meeting to breach the long-standing agreement again and demand the group obtain insurance to indemnify the town at a cost of several hundred dollars.
UAINE’s lawyers filed an emergency motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction, and on Monday, local supporters of UAINE gathered outside holding signs that read “Selectmen – stop abusing Plymouth’s first citizens” and “Stop breaking treaties”.
Judge Brian Glenny heard 90 minutes of arguments. He is expected to issue a ruling soon.
During the hearing, the original agreement wording was dissected minutely. Plymouth’s lawyers argued that it does not specifically mention insurance and that UAINE should apply for it, like other organisers of public events. They added that the “showmobile” – the mobile stage cited in the original agreement – is dilapidated, and the town declined to continue providing a replacement from its own staging equipment, as it had done since 2014.
In a statement, Plymouth said that the town “supports and respects the constitutional rights to freedom of speech and peaceful assembly”. It said it had attempted to find a solution for a year but did not receive a reply from UAINE lawyers until August.
It added: “The town has gone above and beyond to accommodate UAINE’s event, including facilitating accessible parking, assisting elders, identifying locations for meals and extended observances, and coordinating with police and fire officials. The town has continuously demonstrated a willingness to address concerns, offer solutions, and make accommodations at every opportunity. These efforts reflect a genuine commitment to the event.”
In turn, UAINE accused Plymouth of ripping up a 28-year-old political contract, violating its freedom of speech and attempting to force the group, which had been guaranteed the right to choose its own route, to gather at a new location, where members would be “out of sight”.
Plymouth denies trying to change the route and said the offer of the move was based on accessibility, parking, and the use of an existing stage in that location.
After hearing arguments on Monday, Judge Brian Glenny of Plymouth superior court ruled on Tuesday that the 1998 agreement was legally binding and banned the town from requiring insurance or permits for the event.
But he also absolved Plymouth from providing a stage, as it had done for 27 years. The ruling also appeared to open a path for Plymouth to challenge the 1998 agreement again in the future by stating that the 10 Novembervote was legal.
Munro called the ruling “mixed” and vowed to go ahead with this year’s protest.
She said: “Settlers frequently break their agreements with Indigenous peoples. In fact, the US has broken every single treaty it signed with Native Nations. And we know that we can’t count on the courts of the colonizers to give us justice.”
In a statement, Deb Iaquinto, Plymouth select board chair, said: “The Town has tried to work collaboratively to support UAINE’s rights to freedom of speech and assembly.”
She added: “In light of this ruling, the Town remains committed to supporting the National Day of Mourning.”
Pierite, whose organisation Naicob is the commonwealth’s designated liaison for members of the Penobscot, Passamaquoddy, Mi’kmaq, and Maliseet tribes, said the insistence on bureaucracy was being weaponised to erase their unique relationship and history with the town and the United States, and that Native Americans were not just “any other group” holding a parade.
Pierite, a member of the federally recognised Tunica-Biloxi tribe of Louisiana, added: “This isn’t about resiliency of Indigenous peoples. We are going to find a way for National Day of Mourning to happen, but we do need to make sure they are held accountable for this 1998 agreement. Plymouth itself has been a site of government relationships since April 1621 with the original treaty with [Chief] Massasoit [a defensive alliance between Europeans and Wampanoag lasting 50 years].
“Treaties have been endlessly interpreted and reinterpreted over centuries. This is one part of a very long fight.”
